today.text: Liz Truss steps down as British Prime Minister and leader of the Conservative Party amid the country's political crisis, serving for the least time of any British Prime Minister (49 days).
pages: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

today.text: The BepiColombo spacecraft is launched on an Ariane 5 rocket to study Mercury.
Syrian civil war: The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) declare victory in the Raqqa campaign.
Libyan Crisis: Rebel forces capture Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi and his son Mutassim in his hometown of Sirte and kill them shortly thereafter, ending the first Libyan civil war.
The general conference of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) passes the Convention on the Protection and Promotion of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions.
pages: Convention on the Protection and Promotion of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions

today.text: The Sloan Great Wall, once the largest cosmic structures known to humanity, is discovered by students at Princeton University.
Top Gear, the revived popular British TV motoring magazine, premieres on BBC.
Space Shuttle Columbia launches on STS-73.
A 6.8 Mw earthquake strikes the Uttarkashi region of India, killing more than 1,000 people.
A massive firestorm breaks out in the hills of Oakland and Berkeley, California killing 25 people and destroying more than 3,000 homes, apartments and condominiums.

random.extract: Peter Vaško (born 19 May 1987) is a Slovak former professional footballer who played as a midfielder. He is most known for his time with Slovak First Football League side MFK Skalica. He currently coaches the U13 youth category of MFK Skalica.

entry.title: Treble Clef: Unusual X-ray Hot Radio Source
entry.summary:
Explanation: Explanation : What is Treble Clef? This unusual radio structure extends over 2 million light-years and resembles a common musical symbol -- but has its visible light hidden by our own Milky Way Galaxy. Examined in 2004, the nature of VLSS J0318.9+5755, dubbed Treble Clef, remained unknown. Recent observations by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and eROSITA, however, have led to the hypothesis that the Treble Clef central cloud of charged particles was originally expelled by a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy. After the radio emission from those particles faded, they may have been reinvigorated by a shock wave from the collision of two clusters of galaxies. The featured composite image shows radio emission in red, while recently discovered X-rays are shown in blue. Unusual objects like Treble Clef give humanity unexpected clues about how whole clusters of galaxies interact as well as the general evolution of our universe.

Tomorrow's picture: backwards rainbow
